  • Strong hire: Explains the modCount mechanics and other race outcomes, mitigates via the flag, gives a CAS-based snapshot design with cost math, and adds a lint rule plus a stress test, while rejecting COW/synchronized lists with reasons.

questions.contextHtml:
A price-comparison screen ranks offers. Requirement: price ascending, unknown price last, ties broken by rating descending. After release, Crashlytics shows a new crash at 0.4% of offer-screen opens. It only happens on products with many sellers. QA can't reproduce on test products (3–10 offers each). The release also bumped Kotlin from 1.9.24 to 2.0.21, which someone suspects.

java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract!
    at java.util.TimSort.mergeHi(TimSort.java:903)
    at java.util.TimSort.mergeAt(TimSort.java:520)
    at java.util.Arrays.sort(Arrays.java:1424)
    at kotlin.collections.ArraysKt___ArraysJvmKt.sortWith(...)
    at kotlin.collections.CollectionsKt___CollectionsKt.sortedWith(...)
    at com.app.offers.OfferRanker.rank(OfferRanker.kt:19)
data class Offer(val seller: String, val price: Long?, val rating: Float)

object OfferRanker {
    private val byPrice = Comparator<Offer> { a, b ->
        when {
            a.price == null -> 1
            b.price == null -> -1
            else -> (a.price - b.price).toInt()
        }
    }
    fun rank(offers: List<Offer>): List<Offer> =
        offers.sortedByDescending { it.rating }.sortedWith(byPrice)
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every bug, explain why it only crashes on some products, and rewrite it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Kotlin 2.0 changed sorting, revert it", or "add a try/catch and fall back to unsorted". Another weak answer spots the null issue but misses the overflow, or claims stable sorting means the double sort is a bug, without reasoning it through.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • How many offers do crashing products have? I'd expect ≥32, since that's where TimSort starts merging and can detect violations.
    • Are prices in minor units (cents) as Long? This matters for the overflow analysis.
    • Is "ties by rating" also required among null-price offers? It affects the comparator design.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident-level flag, but if a server-side sort exists I can switch the client to trust server order via remote config until the hotfix ships. The hotfix itself is tiny.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. A comparator contract violation in null handling, detected only on big inputs.
    2. Overflow and truncation in (a.price - b.price).toInt() giving inconsistent signs.
    3. The Kotlin 2.0 upgrade. It's a red herring: sortedWith still delegates to java.util.Arrays.sort, and the exception comes from the JDK's TimSort.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A property-based unit test: generate random lists of 0–200 offers with ~10% null prices and prices up to 10^10. Assert sgn(c(a,b)) == -sgn(c(b,a)) for all pairs, and run sortedWith 1,000 times. It reproduces in milliseconds.
    • Crashlytics custom keys for offer count on crash: all ≥32.
  5. Root cause:
    • Bug 1, both null: c(a, b) returns 1 when a.price == null, regardless of b. With both null, c(a,b) = 1 and c(b,a) = 1, which breaks antisymmetry. TimSort with n ≥ 32 merges runs, uses galloping, and can detect the inconsistency. Arrays below 32 use binary insertion sort, which never checks, so QA's 3–10 offer products never crash. The order is just subtly wrong.
    • Bug 2, overflow: a.price - b.price is a Long. .toInt() keeps the low 32 bits. Example: 5,000,000,000 − 0 = 5,000,000,000. The low 32 bits are 5,000,000,000 − 4,294,967,296 = 705,032,704 (positive, by luck). A difference of 3,000,000,000 truncates to −1,294,967,296, which is negative, so a more expensive offer sorts first. Prices in paise or cents for high-value items (≥ ₹2.15 crore, or about $21.5M in cents, i.e. > 2^31 minor units) trigger it. It's rare, but it can also violate transitivity.
    • Bug 3, the design: the two-pass sort is correct only because of stability (the last sort is primary and the rating order survives among equal prices). But it sorts twice (2 x n log n), and the intent is invisible. Anyone "optimizing" it by swapping the order breaks it.
  6. Fix: 
    object OfferRanker {
    private val comparator: Comparator<Offer> =
        compareBy<Offer, Long?>(nullsLast()) { it.price }
            .thenByDescending { it.rating }
            .thenBy { it.seller }            // deterministic order for equal offers

    fun rank(offers: List<Offer>): List<Offer> = offers.sortedWith(comparator)
}
    compareBy uses compareValues, which is null-safe with nullsLast() and uses Long.compareTo (no subtraction). Long term, share one comparator used by both client and tests, and ideally have the backend sort with the same spec.
  7. Prevention:
    • A lint/review rule: no subtraction-based comparators, no hand-written null branches. Use the kotlin.comparisons builders.
    • Property tests for every custom comparator, using sizes ≥ 64.
    • Crashlytics alert on IllegalArgumentException with "general contract" in the message.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • Not catching the exception and falling back to an unsorted list: the wrong order is shown to users and the bug stays hidden.
    • Not -Djava.util.Arrays.useLegacyMergeSort: it isn't a sensible Android solution, and it hides a broken comparator.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What about NaN ratings? → thenByDescending { it.rating } uses Float.compareTo, which has a total order (NaN is greatest). A hand-written < comparison would break the contract again.
  • How would you rank a list of 200k offers? → Same comparator: O(n log n) ≈ 200k x 18 ≈ 3.6M comparisons, roughly tens of ms on a low-end device. Run it on Dispatchers.Default or in SQL.
  • Is sortedByDescending stable? → Yes, it's documented as stable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "general contract" crash sat at 0.2% for two releases because no one could reproduce it. Logging the input size as a custom key took ten minutes and showed every crash at n ≥ 32. A property test then found the both-null branch on the first run.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the Kotlin upgrade. Suggests try/catch.
  • Hire: Finds the both-null contract violation, explains the size-dependent detection, rewrites with compareBy/nullsLast/thenByDescending.
  • Strong hire: Also finds the toInt() overflow with numbers, explains why the double sort works via stability but is fragile, adds a deterministic tiebreaker and property tests, and sets up a Crashlytics custom key for verification.

questions.contextHtml:
A personal-finance app keeps up to 100,000 transactions in memory (loaded from Room at screen start) for an instant-search screen. Users filter by up to 300 selected categories and a text query. Analytics: p50 filter time 220 ms, p95 1.8 s on low-end devices (Helio G35 / 3 GB RAM, ~35% of users). Typing feels laggy, and logcat shows frequent Background concurrent copying GC freed ... lines. The work runs on Dispatchers.Default per keystroke (debounce is handled elsewhere and is out of scope).

fun filter(all: List<Txn>, selectedCategoryIds: List<Long>, query: String): List<TxnUi> =
    all.filter { it.categoryId in selectedCategoryIds }
        .filter { it.note.lowercase().contains(query.lowercase()) }
        .map { it.toUi() }                       // formats currency + date, ~15 µs each
        .sortedByDescending { it.date }
        .take(50)
questions.promptHtml: Make it fast. Quantify where the time goes before you change anything.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add asSequence()" or "move it to a background thread", which it already is. Sequences alone don't fix the O(n·m) in check, and sortedByDescending still forces a full pass. Another weak answer: "increase debounce", which treats the symptom.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does the UI really need only the top 50 by date, or is the list paginated? That decides whether we need a full sort at all.
    • Is the source already sorted by date from Room? ORDER BY date DESC is nearly free in SQL with an index.
    • Is case-insensitive "contains" the real requirement, or prefix and word matching? Prefix or word matching could use FTS.
    • How often does all change versus the query? That tells me what I can precompute.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an outage. As a quick win, I'd ship the two O(n·m)/allocation fixes below behind no flag. They're behavior-preserving and covered by a unit test comparing old vs new output on fixture data.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (with math for n = 100,000, m = 300):
    1. it.categoryId in selectedCategoryIds on a List<Long> is a linear scan, so up to 100,000 x 300 = 30M equals calls on boxed Longs. That alone is hundreds of ms on a low-end core.
    2. query.lowercase() runs inside the lambda, so it's recomputed 100k times, plus note.lowercase() on each survivor. That's up to 200k string allocations per keystroke, which explains the GC lines (a symptom, not the cause).
    3. map { toUi() } before take(50): if 40k rows survive, that's 40k x 15 µs = 600 ms of formatting for 50 visible rows.
    4. A full sort of survivors: 40k x log₂(40k) ≈ 40k x 15 ≈ 600k comparisons, with a lambda per comparison. That's moderate.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A Microbenchmark (BenchmarkRule) with a 100k fixture on the low-end device, isolating each stage.
    • A sampled-CPU trace in the Android Studio Profiler or Perfetto, plus Trace.beginSection("filter.category") around the stages so they show as slices.
    • Memory Profiler allocation tracking for the string allocations.
  5. Root cause: Hidden algorithmic complexity (list contains inside filter), loop-invariant work inside lambdas, and expensive mapping/sorting applied to all rows when only 50 are needed.
  6. Fix:
    • Short term (in memory):
    // Keep `allByDateDesc` pre-sorted once when data loads (or ORDER BY in Room).
fun filter(allByDateDesc: List<Txn>, selected: Set<Long>, query: String): List<TxnUi> {
    val q = query.trim()
    return allByDateDesc.asSequence()
        .filter { it.categoryId in selected }                  // HashSet: O(1)
        .filter { q.isEmpty() || it.note.contains(q, ignoreCase = true) } // no allocation
        .take(50)                                              // early exit
        .map { it.toUi() }                                     // only 50 formatted
        .toList()
}
    New cost: category check is 100k O(1) lookups. contains(ignoreCase = true) uses regionMatches with no new strings. With pre-sorted input and a selective filter, we stop after 50 matches. In the worst case (few matches) it's one pass of ~100k cheap checks, ~10–30 ms. toUi drops from 40k calls to 50 (≈ 0.75 ms). Here the sequence really helps, because we have early termination and no stateful operator.
    • One more boxing fix: Set<Long> still boxes on lookup (categoryId is autoboxed to call contains). If profiling still shows it, use androidx.collection.MutableLongSet (verify availability in your androidx.collection version) or a sorted LongArray with binarySearch.
    • Long term: push the search into SQLite. Use WHERE categoryId IN (...) AND note LIKE ? ORDER BY date DESC LIMIT 50 with an index on date, or FTS4 for word search via Room's @Fts4, and expose it as a Flow/PagingSource. Memory drops from 100k objects (~15–30 MB of Txn + strings) to one page.
  7. Prevention:
    • Keep the benchmark in CI on a fixed device or emulator profile, with a regression threshold.
    • A review checklist item: "in/contains on a List inside a loop or filter" gets flagged, and loop-invariant computations are hoisted.
    • Track p95 filter time in analytics per device class.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • Not parallelizing with chunked + async across cores first. That adds complexity and contention on 4-core devices for a problem that's algorithmic.
    • Not caching lowercase() per row in the model unless profiling still shows string work. ignoreCase makes it unnecessary.
    • Not increasing debounce to hide the latency. That trades UX for a bug.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the product wants sort by amount instead of date? → Pre-sort per supported key once on load (k lists of references, 400 KB each), or use a bounded min-heap for the top 50: O(n log 50).
  • What about Turkish-locale case folding? → contains(ignoreCase = true) does char-wise case comparison, not locale-aware folding. For full Unicode correctness use ICU/Collator or normalize at insert time.
  • What if all changes while filtering? → Pass an immutable snapshot (the Room emission is already a new list), so there's no CME and no torn state.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A search screen's p95 dropped from ~1.5 s to under 40 ms on low-end devices with three line changes: a toSet(), hoisting lowercase(), and moving map after take. The team had been planning an FTS migration for a month. They still did it later for memory, but the urgent problem was algorithmic.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Add asSequence" or "use coroutines", with no complexity analysis.
  • Hire: Finds the List-in O(n·m), hoists invariants, moves map after take, and explains when the sequence actually helps.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies each stage, uses pre-sorted input plus early termination, considers boxing and primitive sets, proposes the SQL/FTS long-term path with memory math, and adds CI benchmarks with per-device-class p95 tracking.

questions.contextHtml:
A messaging app's inbox (View system, RecyclerView with ~30 visible rows) got a redesign in v5.2: each row shows the last message preview, unread count and a reaction summary. Since the release: slow frames went from 6% to 31% and frozen frames from 0.1% to 0.9% (Play Console vitals), concentrated on users with large inboxes. A Perfetto trace during fling shows RV OnBindView slices of 9–14 ms on a Snapdragon 680. The same release migrated image loading from Glide to Coil, which the team suspects.

override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: VH, position: Int) {
    val thread = threads[position]
    val msgs = allMessages.filter { it.threadId == thread.id }      // allMessages: ~20k
    val last = msgs.maxByOrNull { it.sentAt }
    val unread = msgs.count { !it.read }
    val reactions = msgs.flatMap { it.reactions }
        .groupBy { it.emoji }
        .mapValues { it.value.size }
        .entries.sortedByDescending { it.value }.take(3)
    holder.bind(thread, last, unread, reactions)
    holder.avatar.load(thread.avatarUrl)
}
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. Explain how you'd prove the image-loader migration isn't the cause.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Revert Coil", or "use DiffUtil", which doesn't touch bind cost, or "move bind to a background thread", which isn't possible since binding must happen on the main thread. Some say "use sequences" without seeing that the problem is doing O(N) work per row.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • What's the size distribution of allMessages per user? p50 vs p99, because the jank concentration on large inboxes hints at O(N) work.
    • Where does allMessages come from, and is it updated while scrolling (new messages)?
    • Which rows were in the trace, and were the Coil decode slices on the main thread?
  2. Immediate mitigation: If the redesign is behind a flag, roll back to the old row for users with more than ~5k messages. Otherwise ship a hotfix that hides the reaction summary (the most expensive part), while the full fix goes out.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Each bind scans all ~20k messages, then does a groupBy/sort. That's O(N) per bind, and a fling binds several rows per frame.
    2. Coil decoding or transformations on the main thread. Possible, but Coil decodes off the main thread by default, and Perfetto shows the bind slice itself is long.
    3. Layout inflation cost of the new row. That would show as RV CreateView/inflate slices, not OnBindView.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Add Trace.beginSection("bind.filter")/("bind.reactions") around the stages and rerun Perfetto. Most of the 9–14 ms lands in bind.filter and bind.reactions.
    • Disable avatar.load locally with a debug toggle and compare FrameTimingMetric in a Macrobenchmark fling test. If frame times are basically unchanged, Coil is cleared.
    • Allocation tracking during fling: thousands of ArrayList/LinkedHashMap and Map.Entry allocations per frame.
  5. Root cause: Math: filter over 20k elements per bind is 20k predicate calls plus a growing list. A fling binds 2–4 rows per frame, so 40k–80k element checks plus flatMap/groupBy/sort allocations per 16.6 ms frame (8.3 ms at 120 Hz). On a mid-tier core that's several ms per row. The design moved derived-data computation into the most frame-critical callback, and its cost scales with total inbox size rather than with what's visible.
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: precompute per-thread summaries once, off the main thread, whenever messages change.
    data class ThreadRow(
    val thread: Thread,
    val last: Message?,
    val unread: Int,
    val topReactions: List<Pair<String, Int>>,
)

// In the ViewModel/repository, on Dispatchers.Default, when messages change
fun buildRows(threads: List<Thread>, messages: List<Message>): List<ThreadRow> {
    val byThread: Map<Long, List<Message>> = messages.groupBy { it.threadId } // one O(N) pass
    return threads.map { t ->
        val msgs = byThread[t.id].orEmpty()
        ThreadRow(
            thread = t,
            last = msgs.maxByOrNull { it.sentAt },
            unread = msgs.count { !it.read },
            topReactions = msgs.asSequence().flatMap { it.reactions.asSequence() }
                .groupingBy { it.emoji }.eachCount()
                .entries.sortedByDescending { it.value }.take(3)
                .map { it.key to it.value },
        )
    }
}
// onBindViewHolder: holder.bind(rows[position]): O(1), no collection ops
    Feed ListAdapter.submitList(rows). AsyncListDiffer diffs on a background thread with stable ids, so only changed rows rebind.
    • Long term: have Room compute it with SQL (a GROUP BY threadId query for last message and unread count, maintained incrementally) so the app never loads 20k messages into memory for an inbox.
  7. Prevention:
    • A rule: onBindViewHolder and onDraw must be O(1) with no allocation-heavy collection operators. Enforce it in code review and with a custom lint check that flags filter/groupBy/sorted* inside onBind*.
    • A Macrobenchmark fling test with a large-inbox fixture (20k messages) in CI. Track frameDurationCpuMs P90 and P99.
    • JankStats in production with a state tag for the screen.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • Not reverting Coil without evidence: it costs a migration and fixes nothing.
    • Not memoizing per position inside the adapter (HashMap<position, Summary>): that invalidates wrongly on inserts and moves, and it still makes the first bind expensive.
    • Not setItemViewCacheSize(100) as a "fix": it hides the cost during back-scrolling only and increases memory.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• New messages arrive every second in an active group. Do you rebuild all rows? → Rebuild only the affected thread's row (keep byThread incrementally updated). The whole rebuild is O(N) on Default at 1 Hz, which is acceptable at 20k but not at 500k.
  • The designer wants reactions for 1k-member groups. → Cap the work: compute top-3 server-side or in SQL. Client-side groupingBy over 100k reactions per update is waste.
  • Where does Compose change this? → The same rule applies to composition (Q206). Composables can skip, but derived work in their body still runs whenever they recompose.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A redesign that "only added a reaction summary" tripled slow frames for power users. The trace showed bind slices dominated by groupBy. After moving the summary into a precomputed row model, slow frames dropped below the pre-redesign baseline, because the old code had also been filtering per bind, just less visibly.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Reverts the image loader. Suggests background binding.
  • Hire: Identifies the O(N) per-bind filter/groupBy, precomputes row models off-main with groupBy once, and makes bind O(1).
  • Strong hire: Quantifies per-frame cost against the frame budget, proves Coil innocent with trace sections and A/B Macrobenchmark, uses groupingBy/ListAdapter, plans SQL aggregation long term, and adds CI fling benchmarks plus a lint guard.

questions.contextHtml:
A Compose catalog screen (LazyColumn of up to 4,000 products, 1.2M DAU, 40% on 3 GB devices) has a filter chip row, a sort dropdown and a search field. After the v8.0 rewrite from Views, JankStats shows 38% janky frames while typing in search (was 7%). Layout Inspector shows ProductList recomposing on every keystroke, and the Compose compiler report lists ProductList as restartable skippable. The app is on Kotlin 2.0.21 (strong skipping on).

@Composable
fun CatalogScreen(vm: CatalogViewModel) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()   // products: List<Product> (4,000)
    var query by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
    Column {
        SearchField(query) { query = it }
        ProductList(
            items = state.products
                .filter { it.name.contains(query, ignoreCase = true) }
                .sortedWith(state.sort.comparator)
                .map { it.toRowUi(LocalContext.current) },   // formats price, builds badges
        )
    }
}

The team tried converting List to ImmutableList everywhere and saw no improvement.
questions.promptHtml: Why is it janky, why didn't ImmutableList help, and how would you restructure it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in remember" with no keys, or "use ImmutableList and @Stable", or "use derivedStateOf" everywhere. A weak answer doesn't notice that the whole pipeline runs in the composition body on the main thread, and that its output is a fresh list on every recomposition.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is the full product list local (4k rows in memory) or paged? Decides in-memory vs DB search.
    • Is search expected per keystroke, or is a 250-300 ms debounce acceptable? (UX decision.)
    • How expensive is toRowUi (string formatting, Context access)?
    • Do product rows change independently (stock updates), or only on refresh?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a debounce on the query and move the pipeline out of the body (below). That alone typically recovers most frames and is low risk, so it ships as a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. query is read in CatalogScreen's body, so each keystroke recomposes it. The body then runs filter + sort + map over 4,000 items on the main thread, every keystroke.
    2. The result is a brand-new List each time. ProductList takes an unstable List, so under strong skipping it's compared by === and can never skip, so the whole LazyColumn recomposes, and every row's inputs are new RowUi objects.
    3. LocalContext.current read inside map makes the lambda depend on composition state, and toRowUi allocates formatted strings and badges per row.
    4. A stability/ImmutableList problem. This is the red herring: calling toImmutableList() on the new list still produces a new instance, and equals would add O(n) work.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Perfetto/System Trace with Compose tracing (androidx.compose.runtime:runtime-tracing) to see Recompose slices of 20–40 ms on the main thread during typing.
    • The Compose compiler report (reportsDestination) plus Layout Inspector recomposition counts: ProductList count increments per keystroke.
    • Quick arithmetic: 4,000 x (contains ≈ 1 µs + sort comparisons 4,000 x 12 x ~0.3 µs ≈ 15 ms + map 4,000 x ~5 µs = 20 ms) ≈ 35+ ms per keystroke on a Helio-class core, i.e. 2+ dropped frames.
  5. Root cause: Derived data is computed in the composition body. Composition runs on the main thread, on every recomposition of that scope, and any State read inside it (here query) re-triggers it. The output is a new instance each time, so the child can't skip, and 4,000 RowUi objects are rebuilt per keystroke. ImmutableList didn't help because stability was never the bottleneck: the problem was instance churn and where the work runs.
  6. Fix:
    • Move derivation into the ViewModel as a Flow pipeline, off the main thread:
    class CatalogViewModel(repo: ProductRepo, private val rows: RowMapper) : ViewModel() {
    private val query = MutableStateFlow("")
    private val sort = MutableStateFlow(Sort.Relevance)
    fun onQuery(q: String) { query.value = q }

    val rows: StateFlow<List<RowUi>> = combine(repo.products, query.debounce(200), sort) { all, q, s ->
        all.asSequence()
            .filter { q.isBlank() || it.name.contains(q, ignoreCase = true) }
            .sortedWith(s.comparator)      // stateful, but once per change
            .map(rows::toRowUi)
            .toList()
    }
        .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())
}
    (Operator details such as combine, debounce and stateIn are covered in the Flow sections.)
    • In the UI: the search field holds its own text state and calls vm.onQuery. ProductList(rows) receives a stable reference that only changes when the pipeline emits, so it skips for unrelated recompositions. Use LazyColumn { items(rows, key = { it.id }) }.
    • If the filtering must stay in the UI (purely local, small list), use remember(products, query, sort) { ... } or derivedStateOf when the input changes much more often than the result. Never do heavy work unkeyed in the body.
    • Pass Context-dependent formatting through an injected formatter in the mapper, not LocalContext.current inside map.
  7. Prevention:
    • A Macrobenchmark with FrameTimingMetric that types a query into the search field on a 4k-item fixture.
    • Compose compiler reports reviewed on UI-state changes.
    • Review rule: no filter/sorted*/map over data-sized collections directly in a composable body.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • Not ImmutableList as the primary fix: it only matters once instance churn is solved, and large equals comparisons can be slower than ===.
    • Not a stability config marking kotlin.collections.* stable: it hides the symptom, and it's a risky global promise if any code mutates lists.
    • Not derivedStateOf for every derived list: it adds overhead, and the cost problem stays on the main thread.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Filtering must feel instant with no debounce. → Keep the debounce for the server query, but apply a cheap in-memory filter on Default with collectLatest/flatMapLatest semantics so stale work is cancelled, and show the previous results until the new ones arrive.
  • 100k products? → Move search to Room (FTS) with Paging 3. Never hold 100k UI models.
  • Does Baseline Profile help? → It helps startup and first-frame compilation, not this steady-state algorithmic cost.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rewrite from Views to Compose was blamed for "Compose being slow". Two lines moved a filter out of the body and into the ViewModel. Typing jank dropped from 38% to under 5%, and the team stopped blaming the framework.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Wraps in unkeyed remember, adds @Stable and ImmutableList, and doesn't locate the work.
  • Hire: Identifies body-level main-thread work and instance churn, moves it to a ViewModel pipeline with flowOn(Default), and uses stable keys.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies per-keystroke cost, explains the === skipping behavior and why ImmutableList was a red herring, covers remember/derivedStateOf trade-offs, and adds a Macrobenchmark plus a scale plan with FTS/Paging.

questions.contextHtml:
An e-commerce app syncs the user's wishlist from two sources: the local DB cache and a fresh API response. A support ticket says "items I removed price alerts from reappear with the old alert". Another says total wishlist value is occasionally wrong. Metrics: 1.1% of sync runs affected. No crash. The ticket analysis shows it happens when a product appears in both sources.

data class WishItem(val productId: Long, val priceAlert: Long?, val updatedAt: Long)

fun merge(cache: List<WishItem>, remote: List<WishItem>): List<WishItem> =
    (cache + remote)
        .associateBy { it.productId }   // dedupe by product
        .values
        .toList()

fun totalAlertValue(items: List<WishItem>): Long =
    items.map { it.priceAlert }.reduce { a, b -> (a ?: 0) + (b ?: 0) }!!   // hmm

Both lists come ordered by updatedAt ascending (cache) and by server ranking (remote, unordered w.r.t. time).
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs, explain exactly which duplicate wins and when, and fix both functions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "associateBy dedupes, so it works." Or fixing only the crash in reduce. Another weak answer replaces associateBy with distinctBy without checking which element survives.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • What is the conflict-resolution rule: newest updatedAt, remote always wins, or field-level merge?
    • Can the remote list contain duplicates itself?
    • Is a null priceAlert "no alert" or "alert removed"? It affects the sum and the merge.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship the one-line correctness fix (pick by updatedAt) behind no flag. A re-sync repairs stored data, so no data migration is needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. associateBy keeps the last element for a duplicate key. After cache + remote, that's the remote element in remote order. If the remote payload was stale (cached CDN response or a replica lag) it overwrites a newer local change. If remote itself has duplicates, the winner depends on server ordering.
    2. reduce with a nullable accumulator misuse: reduce on empty input throws, and the types don't line up with a Long return (!!, ?: 0 mixing). If the first element's alert is null, a is null and gets treated as 0 only for a, but the first element is never converted from Long? consistently.
    3. A sync-timing race. It's a possible secondary cause, but not visible in this code.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A unit test with the same productId in both lists, in both orders, with different updatedAt. It shows the result is order-dependent.
    • Log both updatedAt values on conflicts in a debug build and count how often the loser is newer.
    • Test totalAlertValue(emptyList()) and a list with a single null alert.
  5. Root cause: "Last wins" is an accident of concatenation order, not a business rule. associateBy silently drops earlier elements without telling you. The semantics: duplicate keys keep the last value in the position of the first occurrence (LinkedHashMap.put). And distinctBy would have kept the first, so swapping the operator flips which side wins (Q190). The sum function is wrong independently: reduce throws on empty input, and mixing Long? into reduce is a type puzzle. sumOf { it.priceAlert ?: 0L } expresses it exactly.
  6. Fix: 
    fun merge(cache: List<WishItem>, remote: List<WishItem>): List<WishItem> =
    (cache.asSequence() + remote.asSequence())
        .groupingBy { it.productId }
        .reduce { _, a, b -> if (b.updatedAt >= a.updatedAt) b else a }  // explicit rule
        .values
        .toList()

fun totalAlertValue(items: List<WishItem>): Long = items.sumOf { it.priceAlert ?: 0L }
    groupingBy(...).reduce resolves each key with the rule written in code and works in one pass without building intermediate lists. If equal timestamps are possible, add a deterministic tiebreaker, such as preferring remote.
  7. Prevention:
    • A unit test matrix: order x timestamp for every merge function.
    • A review rule: any associateBy/associate/toMap on data that can have duplicates needs a comment stating the winner, or a groupBy.
    • A debug-only assertion check(map.size == list.size) where uniqueness is assumed.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • Not distinctBy as a "fix": it just flips the accidental winner.
    • Not sorting by updatedAt first and relying on last-wins. That's fragile, and a future refactor could silently invert it.
    • Not treating a null alert as 0 during the merge. "Removed" and "never set" may differ, so keep nulls in the data and only coalesce when summing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two devices edit the same item offline. → Timestamps from device clocks can lie. Use server-assigned versions or a vector/lamport counter, and treat clock-based merging as best effort.
  • The list has 50k items. → groupingBy.reduce is O(n) with a LinkedHashMap of 50k entries, which is fine. Avoid groupBy here, which would allocate 50k lists.
  • toMap() vs associateBy? → toMap() on pairs is also last-wins. The behavior is consistent across the family.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sync bug looked like data corruption, but it was associateBy after a list concatenation. The rule "remote wins" existed only in someone's head, and it silently failed when a CDN served a stale payload. The fix was three lines plus a table-driven test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Says the code dedupes correctly, or only patches the reduce crash.
  • Hire: Explains last-wins and first-position semantics, makes the winner explicit by updatedAt, and fixes the sum with sumOf.
  • Strong hire: Contrasts distinctBy/associateBy/groupingBy, notes ordering and clock issues, adds order-permutation tests and invariant checks, and discusses null semantics.

questions.contextHtml:
A travel app (900k DAU) exposes search results from FlightRepository as a Sequence<Flight> ("to avoid allocating big lists"). After v3.9: backend request volume on the pricing-enrichment endpoint is up 4.6x, API bills up ~$18k/month, and a StrictMode build shows DiskReadViolation on the main thread. Users report prices flickering between two values. No crashes.

class FlightRepository(private val api: PricingApi, private val dao: FlightDao) {
    fun results(query: Query): Sequence<Flight> =
        dao.loadAll(query).asSequence()                       // already in memory (List)
            .map { it.copy(price = api.blockingPrice(it.id)) } // HTTP call per item, blocking
            .filter { it.price != null }
}

// ViewModel (main thread):
val flights = repo.results(q)
_state.value = UiState(count = flights.count(), items = flights.take(20).toList())
analytics.log("results", flights.sumOf { it.price!!.toLong() })
questions.promptHtml: Explain every symptom from the code, and fix it without making the screen slower.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Cache the API calls" or "add a Retrofit cache", which treats the symptom. Or "use a List instead of a Sequence" with no explanation of why the number is exactly 4.6x. Another weak answer misses that the work runs on the main thread, and calls it a backend problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Average result count per query? (Say 40 candidates after DB load, 20 shown.)
    • Is blockingPrice a blocking Retrofit/OkHttp call? Is this really called on the main thread? (StrictMode says yes for disk. Networking would normally throw NetworkOnMainThreadException, so I'd check whether the ViewModel runs this under Dispatchers.IO and StrictMode flagged a different disk read inside the sequence.)
    • Why do prices flicker? Are prices volatile?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that materializes once (.toList()) before the three uses. That alone removes the multiplication. Roll it out progressively while watching the enrichment endpoint request rate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. A sequence is re-evaluated by each terminal operation. count(), take(20).toList() and sumOf each re-run the entire map (HTTP) pipeline.
    2. The laziness moved I/O to wherever the terminal runs (the ViewModel's caller thread), so the main thread does disk/IO work.
    3. Volatile prices fetched 3 separate times for the same item can differ, hence the flicker between values.
    4. A red herring: Retrofit retries or an interceptor bug. Count calls per query to show they're deterministic multiples.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Count calls per search with an OkHttp EventListener/a logging interceptor. Per query: count() calls once per candidate (40), take(20) calls until 20 pass the filter (~20+), sumOf calls 40 again. Total ≈ 100 vs the intended 40.
    • Check the backend dashboard ratio: the multiplier varies by filter pass rate, which is consistent with ~4.6x aggregated across query mixes with extra retries and paging.
    • StrictMode stack: the violation's frames include SequencesKt...map under the ViewModel call, which shows where the terminal runs.
  5. Root cause: Sequence is a recipe, not a result. Every terminal operation iterates from the source and re-runs every lambda, including the side-effecting network call. This repository returned the recipe to callers who then used it three times. Laziness also defeated the "background" intent: the work executes on whichever thread invokes the terminal. And the copy with a freshly fetched price on each pass returns different values for the same item (prices change), which is the flicker.
  6. Fix: 
    class FlightRepository(
    private val api: PricingApi,        // suspend fun price(id): Long?
    private val dao: FlightDao,         // suspend fun loadAll(q): List<FlightEntity>
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher,
) {
    suspend fun results(query: Query): List<Flight> = withContext(io) {
        dao.loadAll(query)
            .map { it.toFlight() }
            .let { flights -> enrichPrices(flights) }
    }
}
// ViewModel: val flights = repo.results(q)  // List, materialized once
// _state.value = UiState(flights.size, flights.take(20)); analytics: flights.sumOf { it.price }
    (Run price enrichment concurrently with bounded parallelism using async plus a Semaphore, covered in the builders and synchronization sections, and batch it with a single bulk endpoint if the backend allows.)
    • Return List (or a Flow for a stream) from repository APIs. Sequences are for local, pure, in-function pipelines.
  7. Prevention:
    • A repo rule: no Sequence in public APIs of data/repository layers.
    • A lint check that flags a Sequence stored in a val and used by two or more terminals.
    • An OkHttp-level metric of "enrichment calls per search" with an alert on regression.
    • StrictMode in debug and an internal dogfood build.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • Not .constrainOnce() as the fix: it turns a silent 3x cost into a runtime IllegalStateException. Useful as a guard in tests, but not a solution.
    • Not an HTTP cache to hide the repeats: prices must be fresh, and the code would still be wrong.
    • Not removing laziness entirely when it helps: inside results() a sequence with take(20) before enrichment can legitimately avoid 20 HTTP calls, if the requirements allow enriching only the first page.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Only 20 are shown, so could we enrich only 20? → Yes: candidates.asSequence().filter{...}.take(20).map{enrich}.toList() called once. But the count/sum analytics must then use the 20 or be computed server-side.
  • The consumer needs progressive results. → Return a Flow<Flight> using flow { } with bounded concurrency. That's the right async primitive instead of a blocking sequence.
  • Why didn't StrictMode flag the network call? → NetworkOnMainThreadException applies to socket operations when the policy is active. It means the network part likely did run on a worker thread, and only the disk read part occurred on main. That's a clue to check which thread executed each lambda.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "memory-saving" Sequence return type tripled the cost of an API that billed per call. Finance found it before engineering did. The postmortem rule became "repositories return values, not recipes".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds HTTP caching, or blames the backend.
  • Hire: Explains per-terminal re-evaluation, materializes once, and explains the thread/laziness problem and the flicker.
  • Strong hire: Computes call counts per terminal, keeps beneficial laziness inside the function (take before enrich), proposes bounded concurrency/batch endpoint, and adds guards (API rule, metric, lint), while rejecting constrainOnce as a fix.

questions.contextHtml:
A fitness app records heart-rate, GPS speed and cadence at 25 Hz during workouts. The current model keeps three MutableList<Float> per workout in memory for live charts. Sessions are ≤ 90 minutes. Product wants 10x: a "multi-sensor" mode with 10 streams, up to 4 hours, and a live full-resolution chart. Today's numbers: p99 session memory 55 MB heap, GC pause count ~40 per workout, OutOfMemoryError in 0.08% of long sessions on 2 GB devices. Per-device heap limit (largeHeap off) is typically 192–256 MB, and 128 MB on the oldest devices.

class Recorder {
    val hr = mutableListOf<Float>()
    val speed = mutableListOf<Float>()
    val cadence = mutableListOf<Float>()
    fun onSample(h: Float, s: Float, c: Float) { hr += h; speed += s; cadence += c }
    fun averageHr() = hr.average()              // runs every second for the UI
    fun smoothedHr() = hr.windowed(25) { it.average() }   // for the chart, every second
}
questions.promptHtml: Estimate memory at 10x, find what breaks, and design the data layer so it holds up.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set largeHeap" or "store in the DB". It doesn't do the math, and doesn't see that every Float in a List<Float> is a boxed object. It also ignores that windowed(25) per second over a growing list is quadratic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does the live chart need all raw samples, or a decimated view (screens are ~1,080 px wide)?
    • Do we need raw data after the workout ends (export/analysis), and where is it persisted?
    • What are the accuracy requirements: Float or can we store fixed-point shorts?
    • How is backgrounding handled: does recording survive process death?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Persist samples incrementally (batched to a file or Room every few seconds), so a crash or OOM doesn't lose a workout, and cap in-memory history to a window while the redesign lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked / the math:
    • Samples per stream at 25 Hz for 4 h: 25 x 3,600 x 4 = 1,440,000. For 10 streams: 14,400,000 samples.
    • As List<Float>: each element is a boxed Float (12 B header+value, aligned to 16 B) plus a 4 B reference, ≈ 20 B per sample. 14.4M x 20 B ≈ 288 MB. That's well over a 128–256 MB heap, so OOM. Allocation of 14.4M objects also makes GC heavy.
    • As FloatArray: 14.4M x 4 B = 57.6 MB. Fits, but is still heavy next to the rest of the app.
    • Current today: 3 streams x 25 x 5,400 s (90 min) = 405,000 samples x 20 B ≈ 8 MB. The 55 MB p99 comes from the rest of the app, which explains why it was "fine", and that OOM at 0.08% comes from long sessions plus the rest of the heap.
    • Compute cost: windowed(25) { average() } over a list of n samples is O(n·25) every second. At n = 360k (4 h of one stream at 25 Hz is 360,000) that's 9M element visits plus 360k list allocations per second per stream. With 10 streams, 90M visits per second. That is unsustainable and drives GC pauses.
    • hr.average() over n boxed floats each second is O(n) with unboxing.
  4. How I'd verify:
    • Memory Profiler heap dump from a 2 h synthetic session: confirm java.lang.Float instances dominate the retained size.
    • Allocation tracking: millions of ArrayList allocations from windowed, and Float boxing in plusAssign.
    • A Perfetto trace for GC events and the main-thread/worker CPU time of the 1 Hz computation.
  5. Root cause: Boxed generic collections for numeric time series (5x memory plus pointer chasing), O(n) recomputation of aggregates on every tick, and unbounded in-memory retention.
  6. Fix (layered):
    • Storage: a primitive growable buffer. Either a small custom class over FloatArray with doubling growth, or chunked storage of fixed-size FloatArray(4096) blocks (avoids huge contiguous allocations and copy spikes). Use androidx.collection primitive collections if one fits (check the version for MutableFloatList).
    class FloatSeries(private val chunk: Int = 4096) {
    private val chunks = ArrayList<FloatArray>()
    var size = 0; private set
    fun add(v: Float) {
        if (size % chunk == 0) chunks += FloatArray(chunk)
        chunks[size / chunk][size % chunk] = v
        size++
    }
    operator fun get(i: Int) = chunks[i / chunk][i % chunk]
}
    • Aggregates incrementally: keep running sum/count (O(1) per sample) for the average, and a ring buffer of the last 25 samples with a rolling sum for smoothing (O(1) per sample):
    class RollingMean(private val n: Int) {
    private val buf = FloatArray(n); private var i = 0; private var filled = 0; private var sum = 0.0
    fun add(v: Float): Float {
        sum += v - (if (filled == n) buf[i] else 0f)
        buf[i] = v; i = (i + 1) % n; if (filled < n) filled++
        return (sum / filled).toFloat()
    }
}
    • Chart: don't render 1.4M points. Decimate to about 2 x pixel-width points (min/max per bucket, e.g. ~2,000 points). Maintain the decimated series incrementally.
    • Persistence: stream raw samples to disk (append-only binary file or Room batch inserts every 5 s), and keep only the recent window plus decimated history in memory. After the workout, read from disk lazily.
    • Result: raw memory ≈ constant (a few MB) instead of 288 MB.
  7. Prevention:
    • A synthetic 4-hour, 10-stream soak test in CI with a heap limit (use a test device with a 128 MB heap) and a regression check on peak heap.
    • Memory metrics per workout length bucket in production.
    • A review rule: no List<Float|Int|Long|Double> for unbounded numeric series.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • Not largeHeap: it only moves the cliff and makes GC pauses longer on low-RAM devices.
    • Not Room as the live store for chart reads at 25 Hz x 10: write in batches, but serve the chart from memory.
    • Not storing Float at a higher precision than the sensor delivers. If the sensors give 1 bpm and 0.1 km/h resolution, ShortArray fixed-point halves memory again.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The user scrubs back through the whole workout after finishing. → Memory-map or chunk-read the file, and compute decimated tiles by zoom level (like map tiles), so each zoom only reads what it needs.
  • Process killed mid-workout at hour 3. → The append-only log allows recovery: rebuild the aggregates by replaying. Run the recorder as a foreground service so the OS is less likely to kill it.
  • Do you need thread safety? → The sensor callback thread writes and the UI reads. Use a single-writer design with published snapshots (an immutable "recent window" copy or an atomic size read) rather than locks on every sample.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A chart that worked beautifully in a 30-minute test sessions fell over in a 6-hour ultramarathon beta. The heap dump was 70% java.lang.Float. The fix wasn't a bigger heap but changing the representation, because the number that mattered was bytes per sample.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests largeHeap, or "just use the database", with no numbers.
  • Hire: Computes boxed vs primitive memory, replaces List<Float> with primitive storage, and avoids recomputing aggregates over the full list.
  • Strong hire: Full 10x math, chunked primitive series with O(1) rolling aggregates, chart decimation, append-only persistence and recovery, CI soak test with a constrained heap, and rejects largeHeap with reasons.

questions.contextHtml:
Postmortem for last week's incident. An analytics SDK wrapper batches events and uploads in groups of 100. After release 12.3: the analytics backend ingested ~100x the normal event volume for 3 hours (200M events instead of 2M), dashboards showed a fake "engagement spike", the ingestion bill for the day tripled, and the on-call spent two hours looking at retry logic and a reported OkHttp upgrade. Client CPU and battery were also slightly up. The change in 12.3 was a "refactor for readability" of the uploader.

suspend fun flush(events: List<Event>) {
    events.windowed(100, partialWindows = true).forEach { batch ->
        api.upload(batch)
    }
}
// Before the refactor:
// for (i in events.indices step 100) api.upload(events.subList(i, minOf(i + 100, events.size)))

Typical events.size at flush is 3,000.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review: explain the mechanism and the numbers, why it wasn't caught, and what changes you'd make to code and process.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Someone used the wrong function" and stops. A good postmortem answer needs the exact mechanism, math, detection gaps and systemic fixes. Another weak answer proposes blaming the reviewer or "be more careful".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Did uploads have idempotency keys or server-side dedupe? (Evidently not.)
    • What did monitoring show for upload request counts and payload size per flush?
    • Were there tests for flush, and what sizes did they use?
  2. Immediate mitigation (what should have happened): Server-side kill switch or remote-config flag to disable client uploads. Roll back or halt the staged rollout. Ask the backend to quarantine or dedupe by event id for the affected window.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (for the original diagnosis):
    1. A client-side duplication bug. A 100x multiplier is suspiciously close to the batch size, so look at the batching code first.
    2. Retry storms from the OkHttp upgrade. They'd produce a variable multiplier and 429/5xx patterns in logs. There was none.
    3. Backend double-ingestion. It would affect all clients, not just 12.3.
  4. How I'd verify:
    • Group ingested events by event_id: each id appears ~100 times for 12.3 clients (windowed with step 1 gives each event in up to 100 windows).
    • A unit test with 250 events asserting the uploaded batch sizes [100,100,50] and total uploaded = 250.
    • Compare request counts per flush: expected ceil(3000/100) = 30 requests, actual 3000 − 100 + 1 = 2,901 windows at step 1 (plus partial windows at the tail, with partialWindows = true adding 99 more shrinking windows ≈ 3,000 requests).
  5. Root cause: windowed(size, step = 1, partialWindows = false) slides by one element by default. With partialWindows = true it also emits the shrinking tail windows. For 3,000 events that's ~3,000 batches of up to 100 events, i.e. ≈ 3,000 x 100 − (tail) ≈ 297,000 uploaded events instead of 3,000: ~99x. The author wanted chunked(100), which is windowed(100, step = 100, partialWindows = true). The refactor changed behavior while looking tidier. The names are close and both are "batching" in everyone's head. Also notable: the upload count grew from 30 to ~3,000 requests per flush, hence the CPU and battery increase.
  6. Fix: 
    suspend fun flush(events: List<Event>) {
    events.chunked(100).forEach { batch -> api.upload(batch) }
}
    plus a test that guards behavior: 
    @Test fun flush_uploadsEachEventExactlyOnce() = runTest {
    val api = FakeApi()
    flush(List(250) { Event(id = it.toLong()) }, api)
    assertEquals(listOf(100, 100, 50), api.batchSizes)
    assertEquals(250, api.uploadedIds.size)
    assertEquals(250, api.uploadedIds.toSet().size)   // no duplicates
}
  7. Prevention (systemic):
    • Idempotency: each event carries a unique id, and the backend dedupes by id within a time window. This turns a 100x duplication bug into a no-op.
    • Client invariant checks: assert sum(batch sizes) == events.size and log a metric when violated.
    • Monitoring: alert on events-per-session and requests-per-flush deviation per app version (a 100x step change should page within minutes, not hours). Staged rollouts (1% → 10% → 100%) with automatic halt on anomaly.
    • Process: refactors that touch data-transfer paths need a behavior-preserving test written before the refactor (characterization test). "Readability refactor" PRs list the semantic differences of every replaced API.
    • Lint/review checklist: windowed with a batching-intent should be chunked.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • Not "ban windowed": it's the right tool for moving averages. The fix is tests and invariants.
    • Not blaming the author or the reviewer: both operated with a system that lacked a safety net.
    • Not rewriting the uploader into a larger framework during the incident.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Memory side: what if the code had been windowed(100) without a transform on 100k events? → ~99,901 window lists of 100 refs each ≈ 10M references (~40 MB) plus list objects, so an OOM risk on 128 MB-heap devices.
  • Could a Sequence version avoid this? → events.asSequence().chunked(100) is lazy and fine. The bug was a semantic mismatch, not an allocation issue.
  • How do you backfill the corrupted data? → Dedupe on event_id in the warehouse for the 3-hour window, and re-run the aggregates. Dashboards need annotations for the incident.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A one-word change from chunked to windowed passed review because both read as "batching". It was caught by a finance alert on ingestion cost before any engineering alert fired. The lasting changes were idempotent ingestion and per-version volume alarms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Calls it "wrong function" or blames retries/OkHttp, with no numbers.
  • Hire: Explains windowed default step 1 vs chunked, computes the ~99x factor, fixes with chunked, and adds a test.
  • Strong hire: Full blameless postmortem: kill-switch mitigation, request-count math, idempotency keys, per-version anomaly alerts, staged rollout, characterization-test policy for refactors, and the memory implication of windowed.
